subject: physics

items.q: A loudspeaker on a trolley emits sound of constant frequency. The trolley moves at constant velocity along a straight track directly towards a stationary microphone, and has not yet reached it. How does the frequency detected by the microphone compare with the emitted frequency while the trolley approaches?
items.correct: It is higher, and it stays constant while the velocity is constant.
items.misconception: It is higher, and it rises steadily as the trolley gets nearer.
items.why: It matches what listeners report. In the 'Doppler illusion' (Neuhoff and McBeath, 1996) people hear the pitch of an approaching source rising, because the rising loudness is perceived as rising pitch, and everyday descriptions ('the siren gets higher as it comes closer') reinforce the idea. For light, the idea is reinforced by Hubble's law: more distant galaxies do show larger redshifts, but because they recede faster, not because they are farther away. Each wavefront from a source moving at constant velocity is emitted the same distance closer to the observer than the last, so the spacing of the wavefronts, and hence the detected frequency, is constant while the velocity is constant. Distance changes the intensity, not the frequency.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves
items.random_wrong: It is the same; only the loudness of the sound increases.

items.q: In a Doppler ultrasound scan, a probe on the skin emits ultrasound of frequency f into an artery. The blood in the artery flows towards the probe. The probe detects the ultrasound reflected back from the moving blood cells. How does the frequency of the detected ultrasound compare with f?
items.correct: Higher than f, and higher still when the blood flows faster
items.misconception: Equal to f, as reflection leaves a wave's frequency unchanged
items.why: C.3 and GCSE work stress that frequency does not change at a boundary, which is true for stationary boundaries. Students overgeneralise it to moving reflectors. Apply the Doppler effect twice: the moving reflector detects a shifted frequency and then acts as a moving source of that frequency. This is the basis of Doppler ultrasound and radar.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves
items.random_wrong: Lower than f, as the ultrasound loses energy on reflection

items.q: A radar speed detector at the roadside emits microwaves of frequency f along a straight road. The microwaves reflected from a car on the road are detected with a frequency slightly lower than f. What can be deduced about the car?
items.correct: It is moving along the road, away from the detector.
items.misconception: It is at rest, and the microwaves lost energy on reflection.
items.why: E = hf links a photon's energy to its frequency, and 'higher frequency, more energy' is carried over to all waves; a fading sound can also seem to drop in pitch. For a wave, energy lost reduces the amplitude. For photons, a weaker beam has fewer photons each second, each with the same energy hf. In Doppler problems, a lower frequency shows recession, not energy loss.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves
items.random_wrong: It is a long way from the detector, whatever its motion.

items.q: A wavefront diagram shows the sound from a source moving at constant speed through still air towards a stationary observer X. Each wavefront is drawn as a circle centred on the point where the source was when that wavefront was emitted. Compared with the waves the same source emits when it is at rest, how do the waves reaching X differ?
items.correct: A shorter wavelength, and the same speed through the air
items.misconception: An unchanged wavelength, and a greater speed through the air
items.why: Relative-velocity problems (A.1) teach that an object thrown from a moving vehicle carries the vehicle's velocity. Students apply the same rule to waves, which instead travel at a speed fixed by the medium. Waves are disturbances of the medium, and their speed depends only on the medium. If a moving source did add its speed, the wavefronts ahead would be exactly as far apart as for a stationary source; in fact they are crowded together because the speed is unchanged while the source moves between emissions.
items.specStatementText: the representation of the Doppler effect in terms of wavefront diagrams when either the source or the observer is moving
items.random_wrong: A shorter wavelength, and a greater speed through the air

items.q: A wavefront diagram shows the sound from a stationary source in still air as circular wavefronts centred on the source. An observer walks directly towards the source at constant speed. Which statement about the waves and the observer is correct?
items.correct: The wavelength is unchanged, but the observer meets the wavefronts more often.
items.misconception: The observer's motion squeezes the wavefronts, so the wavelength is shorter.
items.why: The moving-source wavefront diagram, with its crowded wavefronts, is usually taught first and is the memorable picture, so students redraw it for the moving observer. Draw the moving-observer case as concentric circles, equally spaced, and move the observer through them. The observer meets the wavefronts at v + u_o (approaching) or v − u_o (receding), so more (or fewer) wavefronts are met each second and the detected frequency changes, while λ is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: the representation of the Doppler effect in terms of wavefront diagrams when either the source or the observer is moving
items.random_wrong: The observer detects the emitted frequency, as the source sets it.

items.q: A spectral line of hydrogen has a wavelength of 656.3 nm when measured in the laboratory. A galaxy is moving directly away from Earth at 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. At what wavelength is this line observed in the spectrum of the galaxy?
items.why:
Students learn the colours of the spectrum as a sequence (red to violet) without attaching wavelengths to them. In everyday life red signals "hot" and "danger" (red-hot metal, the red hot-water tap) and blue signals "cold", so red is easily linked with high energy and hence with high frequency and short wavelength, which reverses the order. Fix the scale: violet about 400 nm, red about 700 nm. Redshift means longer wavelength and lower frequency (recession); blueshift means shorter wavelength and higher frequency (approach).

Working: v/c = (3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 0.0100 (≪ 1, so Δλ/λ ≈ v/c applies). Δλ = 0.0100 × 656.3 nm = 6.563 nm. The galaxy recedes, so the wavelength increases: λ_observed = 656.3 nm + 6.563 nm = 662.9 nm.
items.specStatementText: the relative change in frequency or wavelength observed for a light wave due to the Doppler effect where the speed of light is much larger than the relative speed between the source and the observer as given by Δf/f = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c
items.working: v/c = (3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹)/(3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 0.0100 (≪ 1, so Δλ/λ ≈ v/c applies). Δλ = 0.0100 × 656.3 nm = 6.563 nm. The galaxy recedes, so the wavelength increases: λ_observed = 656.3 nm + 6.563 nm = 662.9 nm.

items.q: A source moving directly away from an observer emits light of frequency 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The observer detects the light with a wavelength 0.20% greater than the wavelength emitted. What frequency does the observer detect?
items.why:
The guide writes the relation as an equality of fractional changes without signs, so it reads as though both quantities rise or fall together. Read Δf/f = Δλ/λ as an equality of sizes. Redshift: wavelength up, frequency down. Blueshift: wavelength down, frequency up.

Working: Δλ/λ = 0.20% = 0.20/100 = 0.0020, so v/c ≈ 0.0020 ≪ 1 and Δf/f = Δλ/λ applies. c = fλ is the same for the observer, so a longer wavelength goes with a lower frequency: Δf = 0.0020 × 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz = 1.0 × 10¹² Hz, and f′ = 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz − 0.010 × 10¹⁴ Hz = 4.99 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (Exactly, f′ = f/1.0020 = 4.990 × 10¹⁴ Hz, the same to 3 s.f.)
items.specStatementText: the relative change in frequency or wavelength observed for a light wave due to the Doppler effect where the speed of light is much larger than the relative speed between the source and the observer as given by Δf/f = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c
items.working: Δλ/λ = 0.20% = 0.20/100 = 0.0020, so v/c ≈ 0.0020 ≪ 1 and Δf/f = Δλ/λ applies. c = fλ is the same for the observer, so a longer wavelength goes with a lower frequency: Δf = 0.0020 × 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz = 1.0 × 10¹² Hz, and f′ = 5.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz − 0.010 × 10¹⁴ Hz = 4.99 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (Exactly, f′ = f/1.0020 = 4.990 × 10¹⁴ Hz, the same to 3 s.f.)

items.q: Every absorption line in the spectrum of a star in our galaxy is at a slightly longer wavelength than the same line measured in the laboratory. What does this show about the star?
items.correct: It is moving away from Earth.
items.misconception: It is a cool, red-looking star.
items.why: The word itself suggests a change of colour, and stellar colour is linked to temperature elsewhere in the course. Astronomy-education research on students' ideas about redshift reports that many take the term literally, as the object appearing red. Temperature changes the overall colour of a star (the peak of its continuous spectrum) but does not move its absorption lines, which are fixed by the atoms. A shift of every line by the same fraction Δλ/λ is a Doppler shift caused by motion along the line of sight.
items.specStatementText: that shifts in spectral lines provide information about the motion of bodies like stars and galaxies in space.

items.q: Over a cycle lasting 12 days, the absorption lines in the spectrum of a star shift to slightly longer wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, shift to slightly shorter wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, and then repeat the cycle. What can be deduced from these observations?
items.correct: The star's velocity along our line of sight alternates in direction.
items.misconception: The speed of the star's light alternately increases and decreases.
items.why: Adding velocities works for balls, and for sound relative to a moving observer, so students extend it to light before they meet the constancy of the speed of light. For light, only λ and f change. Since c = fλ is the same for every observer, a longer observed wavelength goes with a lower observed frequency at the same speed c.
items.specStatementText: that shifts in spectral lines provide information about the motion of bodies like stars and galaxies in space.
items.random_wrong: The star's distance varies; its lines are longest when it is farthest.

items.q: A train approaches a stationary observer at a constant speed of 40.0 m s⁻¹ while sounding a horn of frequency 800 Hz. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the observer hear?
items.why:
In relative-velocity problems (A.1) the closing speed of two objects moving towards each other is the sum of their speeds, so 'towards means add' is carried into the moving-source equation. Decide first whether f′ should be greater or less than f, then choose the sign that gives that result. For an approaching source f′ > f, which needs the smaller denominator, v − u_s.

Working: Moving source, approaching: f′ = f(v/(v − u_s)) = 800 Hz × (340 m s⁻¹)/(340 m s⁻¹ − 40.0 m s⁻¹) = 800 × 340/300 = 906.7 Hz ≈ 907 Hz.
items.specStatementText: the observed frequency for sound waves and mechanical waves due to the Doppler effect as given by: moving source f′ = f(v/(v ± u_s)) where u_s is the speed of the source; moving observer f′ = f((v ± u_o)/v) where u_o is the speed of the observer.
items.working: Moving source, approaching: f′ = f(v/(v − u_s)) = 800 Hz × (340 m s⁻¹)/(340 m s⁻¹ − 40.0 m s⁻¹) = 800 × 340/300 = 906.7 Hz ≈ 907 Hz.

items.q: A dipper vibrating at 4.0 Hz makes water waves that travel across a tank at 0.80 m s⁻¹. A small model boat moves directly away from the stationary dipper at a constant speed of 0.20 m s⁻¹ through the still water. At what frequency does the boat meet the wavefronts?
items.why:
The equations are printed with ± and students substitute mechanically, taking the first sign without predicting the direction of the shift. Predict first: approach raises the frequency, recession lowers it. Then choose the sign that gives that result, and check the answer against the prediction.

Working: Moving observer, receding: f′ = f((v − u_o)/v) = 4.0 Hz × (0.80 − 0.20) m s⁻¹/(0.80 m s⁻¹) = 4.0 × 0.75 = 3.0 Hz. (Check: λ = 0.80/4.0 = 0.20 m; wavefronts pass the boat at 0.60 m s⁻¹; 0.60/0.20 = 3.0 Hz.)
items.specStatementText: the observed frequency for sound waves and mechanical waves due to the Doppler effect as given by: moving source f′ = f(v/(v ± u_s)) where u_s is the speed of the source; moving observer f′ = f((v ± u_o)/v) where u_o is the speed of the observer.
items.working: Moving observer, receding: f′ = f((v − u_o)/v) = 4.0 Hz × (0.80 − 0.20) m s⁻¹/(0.80 m s⁻¹) = 4.0 × 0.75 = 3.0 Hz. (Check: λ = 0.80/4.0 = 0.20 m; wavefronts pass the boat at 0.60 m s⁻¹; 0.60/0.20 = 3.0 Hz.)

items.q: A test vehicle moves at constant velocity along a straight track and carries a siren that emits sound of frequency 500 Hz. A stationary microphone on the line of the track, beyond one end of it, detects the sound at 450 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Taking velocity away from the microphone as positive, what is the velocity of the vehicle?
items.why:
For light the shift does depend only on relative velocity, and in mechanics only relative motion matters, so students assume the same for sound without seeing that the air provides a reference frame. Identify which one moves through the medium. Use f′ = f(v/(v ± u_s)) for a moving source and f′ = f((v ± u_o)/v) for a moving observer; for the same speed they differ, noticeably so when the speed is a sizeable fraction of v.

Working: f′ < f, so the source is receding: f′ = f(v/(v + u_s)). 450 Hz = 500 Hz × 340 m s⁻¹/(340 m s⁻¹ + u_s) ⇒ 340 + u_s = 500 × 340/450 = 377.8 m s⁻¹ ⇒ u_s = 37.8 m s⁻¹ away from the microphone, i.e. velocity = +37.8 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the observed frequency for sound waves and mechanical waves due to the Doppler effect as given by: moving source f′ = f(v/(v ± u_s)) where u_s is the speed of the source; moving observer f′ = f((v ± u_o)/v) where u_o is the speed of the observer.
items.working: f′ < f, so the source is receding: f′ = f(v/(v + u_s)). 450 Hz = 500 Hz × 340 m s⁻¹/(340 m s⁻¹ + u_s) ⇒ 340 + u_s = 500 × 340/450 = 377.8 m s⁻¹ ⇒ u_s = 37.8 m s⁻¹ away from the microphone, i.e. velocity = +37.8 m s⁻¹.

items.q: Does an observer always detect the frequency that the source emits?
items.correct: No. The source emits a fixed frequency, but the frequency detected is the rate at which wavefronts reach the observer, and relative motion of source and observer changes that rate.
items.misconception: The frequency of a wave is fixed by its source, so every observer detects the emitted frequency whatever the motion.
items.why: GCSE work and C.3 stress that the frequency of a wave is set by the source and does not change when the wave crosses a boundary. Students extend 'frequency never changes' to observers and sources in motion. Separate the frequency emitted from the frequency detected. The source's vibration is unchanged, but if the source moves the wavefronts are emitted at different places, and if the observer moves the wavefronts are met at a different rate; either way the detected frequency differs from the emitted one.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a siren passes, is the change heard a change of loudness?
items.correct: No. The loudness does change with distance, but the Doppler effect is a change of frequency, heard as a change of pitch: higher while the siren approaches, lower once it moves away.
items.misconception: The change heard as a siren approaches and passes is a change in loudness, not in frequency.
items.why: In everyday speech 'high' and 'low' are used for both volume and pitch, and the growing loudness of an approaching siren is the most obvious change. Research on learners' ideas about sound reports pitch and loudness being confused. Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude (intensity). An approaching source is heard at a higher frequency because its wavefronts are crowded together; its loudness also increases, but that is a separate effect of distance.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do higher-frequency waves from a vibrating source travel faster?
items.correct: No. In a given medium, sound of every frequency travels at the same speed. A change of frequency is accompanied by a change of wavelength, v = fλ.
items.misconception: A wave's speed depends on how its source vibrates, so waves of higher frequency, such as those ahead of a moving source, travel faster.
items.why: Research on students' understanding of mechanical waves (Wittmann, Steinberg and Redish) found many students believe that a pulse travels faster if the hand producing it moves faster. The idea transfers to 'higher-frequency waves travel faster'. The speed of a mechanical wave is set by the medium (for sound, the air and its temperature). A higher frequency means a shorter wavelength at the same speed. Music heard from a distance arrives with its high and low notes together, which shows that all frequencies travel at the same speed.
items.specStatementText: the representation of the Doppler effect in terms of wavefront diagrams when either the source or the observer is moving

items.q: Is Δλ in Δλ/λ ≈ v/c the observed wavelength?
items.correct: No. Δλ is the size of the change in wavelength, the difference between the observed and emitted wavelengths. The observed wavelength is λ + Δλ (redshift) or λ − Δλ (blueshift).
items.misconception: Δλ is the observed wavelength, so the shift calculated from v/c is itself the wavelength at which the line is observed.
items.why: The equation is usually solved for Δλ, the Δ is easily read past, and the last number calculated is taken as the answer. After finding Δλ = λv/c, add it to (redshift) or subtract it from (blueshift) the emitted wavelength. Check the answer: an observed line should lie close to its laboratory wavelength when v ≪ c.
items.specStatementText: the relative change in frequency or wavelength observed for a light wave due to the Doppler effect where the speed of light is much larger than the relative speed between the source and the observer as given by Δf/f = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a percentage change be substituted directly for Δλ/λ?
items.correct: No. A percentage must be divided by 100 first: a 0.20% change is a fractional change of 0.0020.
items.misconception: A percentage change can be used directly as the fractional change, so a 0.20% shift means Δλ/λ = 0.20.
items.why: Percentages are quoted as numbers (0.20%) and it is easy to carry the number into the equation without converting it to a fraction. Convert first: Δλ/λ = 0.20/100 = 0.0020. Check the answer is consistent with v ≪ c; a result of a fifth of c signals that the percentage was not converted.
items.specStatementText: the relative change in frequency or wavelength observed for a light wave due to the Doppler effect where the speed of light is much larger than the relative speed between the source and the observer as given by Δf/f = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do electromagnetic waves show a Doppler effect at ordinary speeds?
items.correct: Yes. Light, microwaves and radio waves all show a Doppler shift whenever source and observer move relative to each other. The fractional shift is about v/c, small at everyday speeds but measurable; radar speed detectors rely on it.
items.misconception: Only sound, travelling through a medium, shows a Doppler effect; electromagnetic waves travel so fast that there is no shift unless the speed approaches c.
items.why: The effect is introduced with sirens and trains, and at road speeds v/c is only about 10⁻⁷, so students conclude that light needs either a medium or speeds close to c to be shifted. The Doppler effect for light depends on relative velocity, and Δf/f ≈ v/c holds at any speed much less than c. A small fraction of a large frequency is still a measurable frequency difference: this is how radar measures speeds and how astronomers measure the speeds of stars.
items.specStatementText: the nature of the Doppler effect for sound waves and electromagnetic waves

items.q: In the Doppler equations, which is f and which is f′?
items.correct: f is the frequency emitted by the source and f′ the frequency detected by the observer.
items.misconception: f and f′ can be taken either way round, so the detected frequency may be put in place of the emitted frequency when rearranging.
items.why: The prime is a small mark, and when an equation is rearranged to find a speed the two frequencies are easily interchanged. Label the data before substituting: f = frequency of the source, f′ = frequency detected. Then check the direction: f′ > f for approach, f′ < f for recession.
items.specStatementText: the observed frequency for sound waves and mechanical waves due to the Doppler effect as given by: moving source f′ = f(v/(v ± u_s)) where u_s is the speed of the source; moving observer f′ = f((v ± u_o)/v) where u_o is the speed of the observer.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
